content: Hey, I need to think through something that's been sitting on my desk all week. Marco finally booked his Italy trip. He's going February 14-28, 2026 — two full weeks. I knew this was coming, he mentioned it back in December, but now that it's confirmed I need to actually sit down and figure out coverage. Can we just work through this together?

Of course. Two weeks is a significant stretch for a restaurant to be without its head chef, especially when the person who's been driving the kitchen identity from day one is the one stepping away. But you've been open since November — you have three months of operational history, your team knows the rhythms, and you have Haruki. Let's be methodical about this.

Before we get into the details, tell me where your head is right now. Is your primary concern the quality of execution during the absence, the staff morale and authority dynamics, or the front-of-house perception — meaning, do you worry that regulars will notice Marco's gone and that it'll affect how they receive the food?

Honestly, all three, but if I rank them — authority dynamics is the biggest one. Haruki is excellent. He's been Marco's right hand since we opened and before that he trained in Kyoto for four years, did a stage in Modena. He knows the menu cold. But he's 26 and he's never led a kitchen on his own. The cooks respect Marco on a kind of instinctive level. Marco's got this presence. Haruki is technically sharper than people realize but he's quieter, more interior. I just want to make sure we set him up correctly so that the transition of authority is clean, not ambiguous.

That's exactly the right thing to be thinking about, and the fact that you're framing it as 'setting him up correctly' rather than 'hoping it works out' already puts you ahead of most operators who handle this badly.

The quiet, technically excellent second-in-command who hasn't had to assert authority before — that's a specific situation that needs a specific kind of support. A few things tend to matter a lot in these cases.

First, the handover needs to be explicit and public. Not a quiet word in the break room — Marco should address the full kitchen team, ideally in your presence, and say clearly that Nakajima is running the kitchen during his absence, that his decisions are final, and that any questions that would normally go to Marco should go to Haruki. The public nature of that declaration does something important: it preempts the 'let me just check with Kenta' workaround that some cooks will try when they're not sure who's actually in charge.

Second, you need to have a direct conversation with Haruki before Marco leaves — not just a pep talk, but a real operational conversation where you ask him what he's worried about, what decisions he feels confident making alone, and where he'd want you available as a sounding board. The goal is to signal that you trust him completely while also making it safe for him to ask for support without feeling like it undermines his authority.

What's your current working relationship with Haruki like? Do you two talk directly, or does most of the communication flow through Marco?

Mostly through Marco, to be honest. Marco's the kind of head chef who manages upward — he's very good at shielding his team from owner interference and I've respected that. But it means Haruki and I don't have a lot of direct conversation history. I probably need to fix that before February 14. What do you think — should I pull Haruki into a one-on-one now, before Marco leaves, or wait until Marco has done his own handover first?

Do it before Marco leaves, but sequence it carefully. Here's the order I'd suggest.

First, have a conversation with Marco. Tell him what you're planning — that you want to sit down with Haruki directly to make sure Haruki feels supported and that the lines of authority are unambiguous. Ask Marco whether there's anything he wants you to know about Haruki's working style, any current tensions in the kitchen, or any decisions he'd like you to defer until he's back. This respects Marco's role and prevents him from feeling like you're going around him. It also gives you useful information.

Then, after that conversation with Marco but still before February 14, meet with Haruki one-on-one. Keep it practical rather than ceremonial. Tell him you're genuinely excited to see what he does with the kitchen, ask him to walk you through how he's thinking about the two weeks, and listen more than you talk in that first meeting. The goal is for Haruki to leave that conversation feeling seen, not coached.

Finally, the joint send-off — Marco addresses the team with Haruki beside him, passes the keys ceremonially, so to speak, and then Marco is on a plane.

Have you also thought about the compensation question? Haruki is going to be carrying significantly more responsibility for those two weeks. If you haven't already moved to adjust his pay for this period, that conversation needs to happen before February 14 as well — ideally before he starts mentally preparing for the role, not as an afterthought.

Yeah, I've been thinking about that. I don't want it to feel like an afterthought, you're right. I was thinking an 80,000 yen monthly bump for the duration — so prorated for the two weeks, it works out to roughly 40,000 yen extra in his February paycheck. Does that feel proportionate? I don't have a great benchmark for this.

An 80,000 yen monthly bump is a meaningful signal — it's not a token gesture, and the fact that you're prorating it honestly rather than rounding down is the right instinct. Whether it's exactly right depends on Haruki's current base, what the sous chef market looks like in Tokyo right now, and frankly what Haruki himself thinks is fair — though he'll almost certainly accept whatever you offer without negotiating, which is its own thing to be aware of.

What I'd say is this: the number matters less than the framing. When you present it to him, don't say 'we'll give you a little something extra.' Say something like: 'You're going to be the head chef of this kitchen for two weeks. That's a head chef role and it deserves head chef compensation. I want to give you an 80,000 yen monthly bump for this period.' That framing — naming the role explicitly and attaching real money to it — does more to establish authority than almost anything else you could do.

Now let's talk about the rest of the coverage plan. Two weeks is long enough that you probably also need to think about line capacity, not just leadership. Has Marco flagged any dishes or elements of the menu that he considers high-risk without him there? Things where his specific technique or palate-calibration is load-bearing?

Yes, actually. We've been talking about that. The guinea fowl dish is the one we're most uncertain about. It's one of our signature secondi — Marco does a guinea fowl with a Marsala-agrodolce reduction and a celery root fondant, and the timing on the bird is genuinely difficult. The internal temp window is narrow and Marco has an intuition about it that he says is hard to transfer in two weeks. Haruki can execute it but there were two near-misses in the last month even with Marco right there. We're thinking we just drop it from the menu during the coverage period and run a simpler secondi instead.

That's the right call, and I'd make it decisively rather than tentatively. Don't frame it internally as 'we're dropping guinea fowl because Marco's gone' — that subtly codes Haruki's tenure as a degraded version of the restaurant. Frame it as a seasonal menu adjustment. You can bring guinea fowl back when Marco returns and present it as a return to the full menu rather than a restoration after a gap caused by absence.

For your front-of-house team, brief them similarly. If guests ask about the guinea fowl — and regulars who loved it will notice — the answer is 'we've made some seasonal adjustments to the secondi while we highlight some of our other dishes.' That's true, it's not evasive, and it gives the servers something to lean into rather than a gap to explain away.

What are you thinking for the replacement secondi? This is also an opportunity to let Haruki put something on the menu that reflects his own sensibility. It doesn't have to be his dish in a credited way, but if he gets to shape what fills that spot, it gives him ownership over the menu during his period of leadership rather than just executing Marco's vision without the signature element.

That's a really good point actually. I hadn't thought about it that way. He's talked before about wanting to do something with duck — he's interested in a braised duck leg with a local juniper and citrus approach, more of a winter register than the agrodolce. We haven't tested it in service yet but he's cooked it for the team twice and both times it was excellent. Maybe this is the moment to put it on.

Yes. Do that. And tell Haruki explicitly that that's what you want to do — that the two weeks Marco is away are an opportunity for him to show the kitchen and the dining room what he brings, not just a maintenance exercise. The duck braised in his style, with his flavor profile, on the menu under his watch — that's a statement of trust that goes beyond anything you can say in a one-on-one meeting.

You'll want to run a staff tasting before service, obviously. But you were going to do that anyway.

Now — have you thought about line capacity? Marco and Haruki between them are carrying a lot of technical weight. With Marco out, who's handling the volume? Do you have enough skilled hands on the line, or is this a situation where you're going to be running thin?

We're going to be a little thin. Osteria Morishita is not a huge kitchen — we seat 32 covers and we run dinner-only except for Friday and Saturday lunch. Our core line is Marco, Haruki, and then two part-time cooks. One of them, Sato, is solid and has been with us since we opened in November. The other one, Yamamoto, is capable but slow under pressure. So my plan was to bring in a third part-time person specifically for the coverage period. I've already found someone — Toshiya Inoue, culinary school graduate, 23 years old, came recommended by a chef I trust at Azabu Juban. He's worked a few brief stints at small restaurants, nothing long-term, but the technique fundamentals are reportedly strong.

Toshiya Inoue sounds like a reasonable solution for the coverage gap, and the recommendation from a chef you trust is worth more than anything on paper. A few things to think through with him specifically.

Being a culinary school graduate without long-term placement experience means his technique may be cleaner than his service instincts. He'll know how to make things correctly; he may not know how to make them correctly when three tickets drop at once and one of them has an allergy flag on it. Make sure Haruki and Sato both know that Inoue is a support role, not a peer — he should be given tasks where any mistakes are catchable rather than stations where a failure goes directly to the pass.

Also, be deliberate about how you introduce Inoue to the existing team. Bringing in an outsider — even a clearly junior one — during a leadership transition can generate low-level resentment if it feels like the owner is hedging against confidence in the existing team. The framing matters: you're bringing in Inoue because the workload justifies three part-time positions during this stretch, not because you're worried about Haruki's ability to manage. Those things can both be true simultaneously but the order in which you say them matters.

When does Inoue start? Is there time to get him into the kitchen before Marco leaves so Marco can at least see him work and give Haruki a read on him?

Yes, I'm planning to bring Inoue in for February 10 and 11 — two dinner services before Marco flies out on the 14th. That gives Marco a chance to see him and gives Haruki a chance to start building a working relationship with him while Marco is still there to backstop anything. I also want to mention one more thing I'm considering: pausing lunch service for the first week. We only do lunch on Fridays and Saturdays, so we're talking about February 17-21, which includes the Friday and Saturday of the first full week Marco is gone. Just as a precaution. I'm nervous about running a full lunch-and-dinner operation with a new line configuration.

Pausing lunch service February 17-21 as an extra precaution is a sound decision, and I think it's the right call. Here's the reasoning I'd stand behind.

The first full week of any leadership transition is always the hardest. Haruki will be finding his footing as the authority figure, Inoue will be learning the specific rhythms of Osteria Morishita's kitchen rather than the generic rhythms of restaurant work, and Yamamoto's pressure sensitivity is a known variable that you're managing rather than resolving. Running two service formats simultaneously — lunch and dinner — in that specific week multiplies the number of things that can go wrong and compresses recovery time.

Dinner-only gives Haruki control over a single, clean service block each day. The team does mise en place, service goes, debrief. Repeat. That rhythm is learnable fast. Stacking lunch into that means split prep time, split energy, and usually the lunch service suffers because it doesn't have the priority that the evening does — and a bad lunch experience for a guest who shows up specifically for the weekend lunch menu is a real reputational hit.

For how you communicate this externally: update your reservations page and Instagram to note that lunch service is temporarily unavailable February 17-21. If you have any standing lunch reservations already booked for those dates, reach out now, before the week starts, and offer to rebook them at dinner on the same dates or a future date. Don't wait for them to show up.

How are you thinking about communicating all of this to the front-of-house team? The servers need to be briefed on the menu changes, the paused lunch service, and — to the degree appropriate — the change in kitchen leadership, so they can speak to guests with confidence rather than uncertainty.

I was going to do a full team meeting on February 13, the night before Marco leaves. Everyone — kitchen and front of house together. Go through the changes, answer questions, make it feel deliberate rather than reactive. I'd want Marco and Haruki both in the room, and I was thinking Marco could formally introduce Haruki as the person running the kitchen during his absence. Does that structure make sense, or would you change anything about it?

The structure is good. A combined kitchen-and-front-of-house meeting the night before Marco leaves is exactly the right venue for this. A few refinements to consider.

On the Marco introduction of Haruki: yes, absolutely, but be specific about what you ask Marco to say. 'Haruki will be holding things down' is meaningfully different from 'Haruki is running this kitchen and his word is final on everything that happens in this room while I'm gone.' Coach Marco beforehand on the language so he doesn't inadvertently soften it out of habit — head chefs often unconsciously hedge when they talk about their kitchen running without them, because it implicates their own indispensability.

Also consider giving Haruki a moment to speak — not a long one, maybe two minutes — where he talks about the menu changes and what he's looking forward to during the stretch. This serves several purposes. It signals that Haruki has things to say as the leader, it gives the front-of-house staff a chance to hear his voice in authority mode rather than just as Marco's quiet lieutenant, and it starts to build the muscle of Haruki addressing the full team in his own register.

For the front-of-house specifically, I'd walk through: the guinea fowl is temporarily off the menu, here's the replacement secondi and here's how to describe it, lunch service is paused February 17-21, if any guests ask about Marco he's on a planned holiday and returns at the end of February. Brief them on what to say, not just what's changed. Servers who feel informed are confident; servers who feel like they're improvising create a perception gap.

Is there anything you're holding back from the team — anything you're uncertain about — that might come out sideways if someone asks the wrong question at the meeting?

Maybe one thing. I'm genuinely uncertain about whether Haruki wants this opportunity or is simply accepting it because he has to. He's never directly told me he has ambitions beyond sous chef. I don't know if he's quietly hoping to eventually run his own kitchen or if he's content to be a very skilled number two. And I realize I don't know that because I've never asked him. It might change how I frame things to him.

That's one of the most useful observations you've made in this conversation, and it's good that you're naming it before February 14 rather than after.

The honest answer is: you should ask him. Not in the middle of the February 13 meeting, and not as part of a pep talk before the two weeks, but in a separate conversation — ideally before the week of the handover, when there's no performance pressure attached to his answer. Something like: 'I want to ask you something I should have asked earlier. Where do you see yourself in five or six years — do you want to eventually run your own kitchen, or is being the best sous chef you can be the thing that drives you? I'm asking because I want to support the right thing, not just the useful-to-me thing.'

His answer genuinely changes the calculus. If Haruki has ambitions to lead, then these two weeks are a gift — it's a low-stakes, supported, bounded first experience of kitchen leadership, and you can frame the whole thing in those terms. You can tell him explicitly: 'This is good experience for whatever you want to do next. I want you to run this kitchen not just because I need coverage but because I think you should have this on your record.'

If Haruki is content as a sous chef — if the thing he loves is the craft at the station, not the decisions at the pass — then the framing is different. In that case, you'd want to make the two weeks as bounded and supported as possible: clear decision trees for the things he'll face, your phone is on for anything above a certain threshold, and the expectation is execution rather than reinvention. The duck secondi still goes on the menu, but you might pitch it slightly differently — as something you two developed together, not as his solo statement.

The important thing is not to assume. You've been managing around this question for three months and now you're about to give him a significant responsibility. Ask him the question directly. Whatever his answer, it'll make you a better owner for him — and it'll probably make him feel seen in a way that nothing else in the February 13 meeting will.

You're right. I'll have that conversation this week, before things get hectic. Let me try to pull together everything we've discussed so I have a clear action list before we close this out. One — meet with Marco and brief him on my plan to talk to Haruki directly. Two — have a direct one-on-one with Haruki, including the question about his long-term ambitions and the conversation about the 80,000 yen monthly bump for the coverage period. Three — confirm Toshiya Inoue's start date for February 10 and make sure he understands the scope of his role. Four — drop the guinea fowl from the menu during coverage, run Haruki's duck braised secondi instead, do a staff tasting before service. Five — pause lunch service February 17-21. Six — February 13 team meeting with Marco and Haruki both present, Marco formally handing authority to Nakajima in front of the full team. Does that capture it?

That captures it exactly, and the order you've listed them is also basically the right sequence — the Marco conversation unlocks the Haruki conversation, the Haruki conversation unlocks the compensation and the menu decisions, and the team meeting is the final public act that makes all of it official.

A few small additions to layer into those items as you execute them.

On item two — when you talk to Haruki about the 80,000 yen monthly bump, frame it as I described earlier: he's being asked to be head chef, and this is head chef compensation for that period. Make sure the prorated amount is clear in his February paycheck and that payroll is briefed accordingly. The last thing you want is for Haruki to check his paycheck in the middle of the coverage period and find the number he was promised is wrong — that erodes trust at exactly the wrong moment.

On item three — with Toshiya Inoue being a culinary school graduate coming in for the first time, give Haruki some input on where Inoue will be positioned on the line. Haruki is the one who will be managing him daily; he should feel like he had a say in how Inoue is deployed rather than having a new part-timer assigned to him from above.

On item six — ask Marco specifically to say Nakajima's name and use the word 'running' or 'leading' the kitchen, not 'looking after' or 'holding down' the kitchen. The language matters more than it should, but it does matter.

One thing not on your list that I'd add as item seven: a check-in with Haruki at the end of the first week — so around February 20 or 21. Not a performance review, just a fifteen-minute conversation. How's it going, what's been harder than expected, anything you need from me. This signals ongoing support without micromanagement, and if something is quietly going sideways, you want to know on day seven, not day fourteen.

You have a solid plan. Marco will be in Italy, Nakajima will be running Osteria Morishita's kitchen, and you'll have given them both the conditions to succeed. Is there anything else you want to think through before you close this out?

No, I think that's everything. I actually feel significantly less anxious about this than I did when I sat down. Thank you. I'm going to reach out to Marco today and try to get that conversation done before the weekend. And I need to remember — the goal isn't just to survive February 14-28, 2026. It's to give Haruki a real experience of leading this kitchen. If we do that right, we come out of it with a stronger team than we went in with.

That's exactly the right way to hold it. Two weeks from now, if you've executed this plan, you won't just have made it through Marco's vacation — you'll have given Nakajima his first real experience as a kitchen leader, you'll have a better direct relationship with him as an owner, you'll have Toshiya Inoue integrated into the team with some real service hours behind him, and you'll know more about what your kitchen can do without its most senior person than you knew before.

Restaurants find out who they really are during the periods that weren't supposed to be tests. February 14-28, 2026 is going to teach you something about Osteria Morishita that three months of normal operation couldn't. Haruki running the kitchen, a new dish on the menu that came out of his sensibility, the team holding together without the person whose presence has defined the room since November — that's worth knowing.

Good luck with the Marco conversation today. And enjoy the fact that for two weeks, Osteria Morishita at 3-14-7 Higashi-Azabu is going to be Haruki Nakajima's restaurant. Let him feel that.
